source: Cox & D'Antonio 3e Table C.1, PDF pages 545-546 (printed pp. 488-489)
about:
The eighteen rows of Table C.1, "3D BEM predictions normal incidence", print over two pages, sideways on the page, in three bold groups with a sketch each: sinusoidal cross-section, triangular cross-section, and rectangular cross-section battens, the third with a width w as well as a height and a period. The columns are the one-third octave bands from 250 Hz to 4 kHz, and the values are correlation scattering coefficients at normal incidence, dimensionless. Every cell is filled.

These numbers were computed rather than measured. Section 5.3.7, “Scattering coefficient table” (PDF page 222, printed p. 165), says Tables C.1 and C.2 "were created for single-plane diffusers (3 m x 3 m) predicted using a 3D BEM", that they "show how the normal and random incidence correlation scattering coefficients vary between different surface topologies (sinusoidal, triangular, and rectangular) for a variety of different heights", and that "below 250 Hz, the scattering coefficients should be taken to be 0", which is why the table starts there. The same section warns that "the formulation for the correlation scattering coefficient needs to be revised for surfaces that partially absorb, because the current formulation interprets any absorption as being scattering".

Both this table and Table C.2 print a source line under their last group: "Source: Lee, H., Sakuma, T., Appl. Acoust., 88, 129-136, 2015.", with a marker into the appendix's one-item reference list on PDF page 553 (printed p. 496), which spells it "H. Lee and T. Sakuma, "Numerical characterization of acoustic scattering coefficients of one-dimensional periodic surfaces", Appl. Acoust., 88, 129-36 (2015)". The two spellings of the page range differ, 129-136 against 129-36; the reference list's is the one carried here.

Each group closes with a row labelled "h/L = 20", "h/L = 25" or "h/L = 15", and those are rows with values and not headings. The label cannot be read as it stands: every surface of every group is h = 2 to 10 cm with L = 20 cm, so h/L runs from 0.1 to 0.5 and never reaches 15. Read as a percentage the labels resolve, and the table proves it: the sinusoidal "h/L = 20" carries the same thirteen values as its own "h = 4 cm, L = 20 cm", which is a ratio of 20%. The other two match no row of their group and fall between two of them, so they are the h = 5 cm and h = 3 cm cases, neither of which is tabulated. The book says nothing about these rows anywhere: the string "h/L" appears in its tables and nowhere else in its prose.

Those same rows are the only ones printed without their trailing zeros, so that a cell reads "0" where its neighbours read "0.00", "0.9" where they read "0.90", and, in one cell of "h/L = 25", a bare "1". They are kept as printed. In this table the values are set flush left in their columns while Tables C.2 and C.3 centre theirs, which is what makes those short cells look like empty ones.
